groups.text: Vert X runs on Netty.
A Vert X instance starts a group of Netty event loops, by default twice the number of cores: eight on a four-core machine.
What Vert X adds is a rule on top of those loops: the context.
A context is the home of a piece of code, and it decides the thread that runs it.
Each verticle you deploy gets its own context, tied to one event loop for life.
Every handler it registers, for HTTP, timers or the event bus, runs on that context.
So a verticle's code runs on one thread, one task at a time.
Three events for verticle A arrive at the same moment.
The loop runs them one after another, never at once.
So A's field, approved, needs no lock.
The catch: that thread is shared.
Verticle B's context sits on the same loop.
Now A's handler makes a five hundred millisecond JDBC call, right on the loop.
The loop can do nothing else until it returns, so B's requests wait, though B did nothing wrong.
executeBlocking moves the blocking part to a worker thread.
A's handler returns at once, and the loop is free for B.
When the query is done, the Future completes back on A's context, on loop zero.
So the reply runs on A's own thread, and A's state still needs no lock.
One catch: executeBlocking is ordered by default, so calls from one context still run one at a time.
Pass false when they are independent.
In the lesson's demo, four five hundred millisecond queries took two seconds ordered, and half a second with false.
Vert X calls this the golden rule: don't block the event loop.
A checker thread looks every second, and warns when one task has held a loop for more than two seconds.
